A '''permutation''' represents a particular way of arranging the elements in a [[set]].

== Formal definition ==

Let $S$ be a set.

Any [[Function#Formal_definition|bijective function]]

$$
\sigma: S \to S
$$

is a '''permutation''' of set $S$.

{{Hidden example}}
Set $\{1,2,3\}$ has six permutations:

$$
\begin{cases}
\sigma_1(1)=1,\quad \sigma_1(2)=2,\quad \sigma_1(3)=3,\\
\sigma_2(1)=1,\quad \sigma_2(2)=3,\quad \sigma_2(3)=2,\\
\sigma_3(1)=2,\quad \sigma_3(2)=1,\quad \sigma_3(3)=3,\\
\sigma_4(1)=2,\quad \sigma_4(2)=3,\quad \sigma_4(3)=1,\\
\sigma_5(1)=3,\quad \sigma_5(2)=1,\quad \sigma_5(3)=2,\\
\sigma_6(1)=3,\quad \sigma_6(2)=2,\quad \sigma_6(3)=1.
\end{cases}
$$
{{End hidden}}

== Notation ==

In general, a permutation for set $S=\{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n\}$ can be noted:

$$
\sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
s_1 & s_2 & \cdots & s_n \\
\sigma_{s_1} & \sigma_{s_2} & \cdots & \sigma_{s_n}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

{{Hidden example}}
The permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$ are:

$$
\operatorname{Perm}(\{1,2,3\})=
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&2&3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&1&3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\3&2&1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&3&2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&3&1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\3&1&2\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$
{{End hidden}}

== Special permutations ==

=== {{anchor|Identity_permutation}}Identity permutation: $\sigma_{id}(s)=s$ ===

The '''identity permutation''' for set $S=\{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n\}$ is

$$
\sigma_{id} =
\begin{pmatrix}
s_1 & s_2 & \cdots & s_n \\
s_1 & s_2 & \cdots & s_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

{{Hidden example}}
The identity permutation for $\{1,2,3\}$ is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&2&3 \\
1&2&3
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
{{End hidden}}

=== Transposition ===

A '''transposition''' is a permutation that swaps only two elements and do nothing to the rest of the elements.

i.e.,

if
$$
\exists i,j \in \{1,2,\cdots,n\}:
\begin{cases}
\tau(s_i)=s_j \\
\tau(s_j)=s_i \\
\tau(s_k)=s_k ,& \forall k \in \{1,2,\cdots,n\}, k \ne i \lor j
\end{cases}
$$

then $\tau$ is a transposition of set $\{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n\} $.

=== {{anchor|Symmetric_groups}}Symmetric groups $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ ===

$\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3,\cdots,\sigma_{n!}\}$, the '''set''' of all permutations for $\{1,2,3,\cdots,n\}$, is known as the '''symmetric group''' of degree n, denoted by $\mathcal{S}_n$.

== Properties ==

=== {{anchor|Counting_permutations}}$n$ elements $\Rightarrow $ $n!$ permutations ===

For any set $S:|S|=n$:

$$
|\operatorname{Perm}(S)|=n!
$$

=== Inversion pairs ===

Let $A$ be a set and

$$
\sigma_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_1&a_2&\cdots&a_n \\
b_1&b_2&\cdots&b_n
\end{pmatrix},\, a,b \in A
$$

be one of its permutation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\forall a_i,a_j &: i,j \in \{1,2,\cdots,n\}, \\
\exists b_p,b_q &: p,q \in \{1,2,\cdots,n\} \Rightarrow b_p=a_i,\ b_q=a_j \\
&\text{if } p \lt q \land i \gt j \\
&\Rightarrow (p,q) \text{ is an } \textbf{inversion pair}
\end{aligned}
$$

The number of unique inversion pairs in arbitrary permutation $\sigma$ is often denoted by $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)$

If $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$, $\sigma$ is called an '''even permutation'''. Elsewise it is an '''odd permutation'''.

{{Hidden example}}
One permutation for $\{a,b,c\}$

$$
\sigma=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b&c \\
b&c&a
\end{pmatrix}
$$

has inversion pairs $(1,3)$ and $(2,3)$. It is therefore an even permutation since

$$
\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)=2 \equiv 0 \pmod 2
$$ 
{{End hidden}}

=== {{anchor|Sign_function}}$\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)$ ===

$$
\operatorname{sign}(\sigma) = (-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}
$$

<blockquote>
All even permutations have sign $+1$ and all odd ones sign $-1$.
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
For any [[#transposition|transposition]], $\operatorname{sign}(\tau)=-1$
</blockquote>

<ref>{{#cite:Q2231}}</ref>

== Composition ==

Since each permutation is a [[function]], they can be composed:

$$
\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
s_1 & s_2 & \cdots & s_n \\
\sigma_1(\sigma_2(s_1)) & \sigma_1(\sigma_2(s_2)) & \cdots & \sigma_1(\sigma_2(s_n))
\end{pmatrix}
$$

=== Composition properties ===

==== {{Anchor|existence of composite permutation}}Compositions of permutations are permutations ====

If $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ are permutations of $S$, so is $\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2$

{{Hidden proof}}
Since $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ are permutations of $S$, by [[#formal definition|definition]]

$$
\sigma_1:S \to S \\
\sigma_2:S \to S
$$ 

Hence by [[Function#Composition|composition]]

$$
\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2: S \to S
$$
which is a bijection of $S$ to $S$. 

By [[#Formal_definition|definition]], any bijection of $S \to S$ is also a permutation of $S$, so $\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2$, is also a permutation of $S$.
{{End hidden}}

==== {{anchor|sign composition}} $\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2)= \operatorname{sign}(\sigma_1)\cdot\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_2)$ ====

Where $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ are permutations of the same set.

{{Hidden proof}}

Let $S=\{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n\}$ be a set, $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ two of its permutations.

For each pair of elements $s_a,s_b \in S: a \lt b$,

$$
\exists s_i,s_j \in S, i \lt j: \{\sigma_2(s_i),\sigma_2(s_j)\}=\{s_a,s_b\} \\
\exists s_m,s_k \in S: \sigma_1(s_a)=s_m,\sigma_1(s_b)=s_k, \\
\exists s_c,s_d \in S: (\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2(s_i)=s_c,(\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2)(s_j)=s_d, \\
$$

Define [[boolean-valued function]]s $I,P,Q$ that

$$
I_{a,b}=
\begin{cases}
1 ,& c \gt d \\
0 ,& c \lt d
\end{cases},\, 
P_{a,b}=
\begin{cases}
1 ,& m \gt k \\
0 ,& m \lt k
\end{cases},\,
Q_{a,b}=
\begin{cases}
1 ,& s_a=\sigma_2(s_j),s_b=\sigma_2(s_i)\\
0 ,& s_a=\sigma_2(s_i),s_b=\sigma_2(s_j)
\end{cases},\\
$$

* If $Q=0$, $s_a=\sigma_2(s_i),s_b=\sigma_2(s_j)$

$$
I=1 \iff P=1
$$
* Else $Q=1$, $s_a=\sigma_2(s_j),s_b=\sigma_2(s_i)$

$$
I=1 \iff P=0
$$

Hence,

$$
I_{a,b} \equiv P_{a,b}+Q_{a,b} \pmod 2 \text{ for any } s_a,s_b \in S,\, a \lt b \\
\therefore \sum^{s_a,s_b \in S}_{a<b} I_{a,b} \equiv \sum^{s_a,s_b \in S}_{a<b} P_{a,b} + \sum^{s_a,s_b \in S}_{a<b} Q_{a,b} \pmod 2 \\
\therefore \operatorname{inv}(\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2) \equiv \operatorname{inv}(\sigma_1)+\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_2) \pmod 2 \\
\therefore (-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2)} \equiv (-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_1)+\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_2)} \\
\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_1 \circ \sigma_2)=\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_1)\cdot\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_2) \\
$$
{{End hidden}}

==== {{Anchor|transposition sign composition}}$\operatorname{sign}(\tau \circ \sigma)=-\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)$ ====

Where $\tau$ is a [[#transposition|transposition]] and $\sigma$ is any permutation of same set $S$.

{{Hidden proof}}
From [[#transposition|definition]], $\operatorname{sign}(\tau)=-1$.

From [[#sign composition|property]],

$$
\operatorname{sign}(\tau \circ \sigma)=\operatorname{sign}(\tau) \cdot \operatorname{sign}(\sigma) = - \operatorname{sign}(\sigma)
$$

{{End hidden}}

== {{anchor|inverse permutation}}Inverse permutation $\sigma^{-1}$ ==

If $\sigma$ is a permutation of set $S$, $\sigma^{-1}$ is also a permutation of set $S$.

{{Hidden proof}}
Since for any set $S$, $\sigma:S \to S$ is a bijection, $\sigma^{-1}: S \to S$ is also a bijection of $S$ to $S$. 

By [[#Formal_definition|definition]], any bijection of $S \to S$ is also a permutation of $S$, so $\sigma^{-1}$, is also a permutation of $S$.
{{End hidden}}

=== Inverse permutation properties ===

==== {{Anchor|inverse composition}}$\sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma=\sigma_{id}=\sigma \circ \sigma^{-1}$ ====

for any permutation $\sigma$.

{{Hidden proof}}
Let $S=\{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_n\}$ be a set, $\sigma$ be any one of its permutations.

By [[#Formal_definition|definition]],

$$
\forall s_a \in S: \exists s_b \in S, s_a \mapsto s_b
$$

By [[Function#Formal_definition|definition]],

$$
\sigma^{-1}: s_b \mapsto s_a \\
\therefore (\sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma)(s_a)=\sigma^{-1}[\sigma(s_a)]=\sigma^{-1}(s_b)=s_a,\, \forall s_a \in S \\
\therefore \sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma = \sigma_{id}
$$

Let $\sigma'=\sigma^{-1}$, then $\sigma'^{-1}=\sigma$. Since $\sigma$ is any permutation of $S$, $\sigma'$ can also be any permutation of $S$

$$
(\sigma' \circ \sigma'^{-1})(s_a)=\sigma'[\sigma'^{-1}(s_a)]=\sigma'(s_b)=s_a,\, \forall s_a \in S
\therefore \sigma' \circ \sigma'^{-1}=\sigma_{id}
$$

Hence

$$
\sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma=\sigma_{id}=\sigma \circ \sigma^{-1}
$$

{{End hidden}}

==== $\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)=\operatorname{sign}(\sigma^{-1})$ ====

for any permutation $\sigma$.

{{Hidden proof}}
From [[#inverse composition|property]],

$$
\sigma^{-1} \circ \sigma=\sigma_{id}
$$

From [[#sign composition|property]],

$$
\operatorname{sign}(\sigma^{-1} ) \cdot \operatorname{sign}(\sigma)=\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_{id})=1
$$

Hence

$$
\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)=\operatorname{sign}(\sigma^{-1})
$$

{{End hidden}}
